mcqs.question: You run `grep foo file | sort | uniq -c` and press Ctrl+C. What actually happens?
options: Only uniq -c, the last command in the pipeline, receives SIGINT
Only grep, the first command in the pipeline, receives SIGINT
All three processes receive SIGINT, because the shell placed them all in the same process group
Nothing happens until the pipeline finishes naturally
mcqs.explanation: The shell puts every process in a pipeline into one process group, and signal delivery to a group hits every member at once — so all three commands are interrupted together. Neither 'only the first' nor 'only the last' matches how process-group signal delivery works, and Ctrl+C isn't deferred until completion.

mcqs.question: A background job tries to read from standard input while another job is in the foreground. What happens to the background job?
options: It reads the input successfully alongside the foreground job
It silently receives empty input and continues
It crashes immediately with a fatal error
It is automatically stopped with SIGTTIN, since only the foreground process group can read from the terminal
mcqs.explanation: The kernel prevents two process groups from racing over the same terminal input by stopping the background job with SIGTTIN when it attempts a read. It doesn't get to read alongside the foreground job, doesn't crash, and doesn't get silently fed empty input.

mcqs.question: Why does the kernel send SIGHUP to a session when its controlling terminal disconnects?
options: To notify the user that their internet connection is unstable
To force all processes in the session to save their state before continuing to run
To give processes in that session a chance to terminate, so background jobs from closed sessions don't accumulate forever on the machine
SIGHUP is sent only to processes actively writing to the terminal at that moment
mcqs.explanation: SIGHUP exists so a session's processes clean up (by default, terminate) when the terminal that spawned them goes away, preventing indefinite accumulation of orphaned jobs. It isn't a connectivity notification, doesn't force continued execution with saved state, and isn't limited to processes actively writing at that instant.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between running `nohup ./task.sh &` versus running `./task.sh &` and then `disown %1`?
options: There is no difference — both are exactly equivalent in every case
nohup makes the process ignore SIGHUP from the moment it starts; disown only removes it from the shell's own job table, so the shell specifically won't be the one sending it SIGHUP
disown is strictly stronger than nohup and makes a process immune to every signal
nohup only works for shell scripts, never for compiled binaries
mcqs.explanation: nohup sets SIGHUP-ignoring behavior before the program runs, while disown just detaches the job from the shell's tracking so the shell exiting doesn't trigger it — a narrower guarantee. disown isn't a blanket immunity to all signals, nohup works on any executable, and the two approaches aren't equivalent.

mcqs.question: You start `./deploy.sh &` over SSH and immediately close the terminal. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The script continues running normally, since & backgrounds it permanently
The script is paused and resumes automatically the next time you SSH in
The script receives SIGHUP when the session's controlling terminal disconnects and is likely terminated mid-execution
The script is unaffected, because SIGHUP only targets foreground jobs
mcqs.explanation: Backgrounding with & only affects foreground/background status within the live session — it does nothing to protect against SIGHUP when the session's terminal disconnects, so the job is typically killed along with the rest of the session. It doesn't auto-pause-and-resume, and SIGHUP targets the whole session, not just foreground jobs.
